title: Hand drill
prompt: A labelled teaching model of the page 66 hand drill is held above a wood specimen. Crank turns the large crown wheel and the engaged bevel pinion so the chuck and bit rotate faster than the crank. Feed uses an external hand to press the spinning cutting tip into the wood while chips move out along the spiral flutes. Withdraw uses the hand to lift the bit out while the crank turns. See-through exposes the gear teeth, pinions, spindle, chuck and bit. Keep the supporting hand and specimen as teaching fixtures. Do not add an electric motor, hammer action or an automatic feed.
blurb: A teaching adaptation of the page 66 hand drill shows bevel gearing, hand-fed cutting and chips travelling along spiral flutes.
chapter: Part 1: The Mechanics of Movement / Screws
truthNotes: Illustrative 32:8 crown and bevel gearing gives four bit turns per crank turn. The lower pinion drives the spindle; the opposing upper pinion freewheels on a sleeve.
The external supporting hand provides all feed and withdrawal. Crank alone does not translate the tool.
Hand and specimen are teaching fixtures, excluded from anatomy. Scale and animation speed are adapted. Hole depth is a model quantity in millimetres, independent of display scale.
Chips are enlarged illustrative particles, generated by new cutting only. The hole and ejected chips persist after withdrawal.
See-through fades the frame, grip, chuck shell, hand and specimen to expose existing solid anatomy. No motor, hammer action, automatic feed or invented label hardware.
1988 remains inaccessible and unverified. No complete edition-union claim.
After feed reaches its depth, the hand holds the tool still and the crank continues until the last chips clear the flutes.
